You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

content = """ARC task-529220ca VERIFIED CORE RULE (21x21 -> 3x5): Three horizontal bands follow full separator rows, in top-to-bottom output-row order. Each band has either no object or a 3-column crenellated object in the separator color. Output column 3 is always 9. Empty band => [0,0,0,9,0]. Nonempty band => left-aligned run of its object/separator color in columns 0..2, then 9. RUN LENGTH IS DETERMINED BY RANKING OBJECT HEIGHTS ACROSS THE NONEMPTY BANDS, NOT ceil(height/2) OR BAND CAPACITY. With three objects: shortest ->1, middle ->2, tallest ->3. With two objects: shorter ->2, taller ->3. This fits every saved demo: D1 heights 4,5 ->2,3; D2 heights 3,5,7 ->1,2,3; D3 heights 7,3,4 ->3,1,2; D4 heights 6,5 ->3,2; D5 heights 6,5 ->3,2; D6 heights 3,5 ->2,3; D7 heights 1,3 ->2,3; D8 heights 4,5 ->2,3. A single gray 5 goes in output column 4. Gray row depends on horizontal position relative to objects and is not fully generalized; robust observed case: gray left of all objects => bottom output row. Gray right of all objects with three nonempty bands => top row (D2). In two-object/blank-band cases gray placement varies, so use demos if unclear.

NEW SOLVED TEST (one wrong attempt caused by accidentally reversing shortest/middle ranks): b0 azure8 h4/cap4 at x12, b1 orange7 h2/cap5 at x16, b2 magenta6 h5/cap5 at x17, gray5 x10 left of all. Heights rank h2 shortest ->1, h4 middle ->2, h5 tallest ->3. CORRECT OUTPUT: [[8,8,0,9,0],[7,0,0,9,0],[6,6,6,9,5]]. Initial incorrect output had top run1 and middle run2. Always explicitly sort heights and map shortest/middle/tallest before submitting.

Other saved gray examples: D3 gray x8, object x12,x10,x2 => gray bottom; D4 gray x12, objects x15,x2 => gray middle; D5 gray x6 left of objects x13,x12 => bottom; D6 gray x17 right of objects x4,x13 => middle (b1); D7 gray x13 right of x9,x11 => bottom; D8 gray x17 with objects x17,x0 => bottom. Solved earlier test: first band empty, blue1 h3 x?, red2 h7, gray x3 left of both => bottom, output [[0,0,0,9,0],[1,1,0,9,0],[2,2,2,9,5]]."""
